rv.q: A female secret agent’s extraordinary courage never quite comes to life in a drama that struggles to find tension in her high-stakes story.

Though the play feels unfocused, it remains a necessary reminder – as we once again face the prospects of surging authoritarianism and war in Europe – of the bravery and sacrifice needed to overcome evil.
An absorbing, kinetic, quietly devastating play, this reaches the silence of great writing from a great subject.
I think, being the writer she was, she would have liked her life immortalised in a play, especially one as good as this.

But as a theatrical event, it needs a couple of male actors, some more steely confrontations and more insight to how she operated for those four months at large in France to have a better sense of what a remarkable woman she was.

This play will appeal to those with a particular interest in stories of heroism during World War Two or those that like their plays to be fairly flat in their presentation but end in an emotional way.

For those unfamiliar with Noor-un-Nisa Inayat Khan, the show offers little other than a fleeting, face-value look into the life of a woman who gave her life for her country, attempting to aid the war effort in World War 2.
Ultimately, a small and quiet light is a disappointing production of a story that deserves to be more compelling.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this biographical drama about WWII spy Noor Inayat Khan. While her heroic story inspires, most find the fractured, meandering structure struggles to generate tension, though some praise its quiet reverence.
